classification.difficultyReason: Two cubic models need a quadratic solve and the second-derivative test. Part b has two stationary points, so the student must pick the maximum and then evaluate the profit. Part a needs unit conversion from hundreds. There is no endpoint comparison, so it is easier than the global-extremum tasks.

content.prompt: Find the local maximum in each of these business models.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A Brisbane bakery's daily profit is modelled by $P(x)=x^3-36x^2+324x$ dollars, where $x$ is the number of pies sold, in hundreds. How many pies give a local maximum profit?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P'(x)&=3x^2-72x+324\\0&=3(x^2-24x+108)\\0&=3(x-6)(x-18)\\x&=6\text{ or }18.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}P''(x)&=6x-72\\P''(6)&=-36<0\\P''(18)&=36>0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=6$ gives a local maximum. As $x$ counts hundreds of pies, $6\times100=600$ pies.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A Gold Coast surf school's daily profit is modelled by $P(x)=-x^3+18x^2-60x$ dollars, where $x$ is the number of lessons booked. What is the local maximum profit?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P'(x)&=-3x^2+36x-60\\0&=-3(x^2-12x+20)\\0&=-3(x-2)(x-10)\\x&=2\text{ or }10.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}P''(x)&=-6x+36\\P''(2)&=24>0\\P''(10)&=-24<0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=10$ gives a local maximum.
$$\begin{align*}P(10)&=-1000+1800-600\\P(10)&=200.\end{align*}$$
The local maximum profit is $\$200$.
